description:
Somos un equipo de entusiastas de la tecnología, la inteligencia artificial y la exploración espacial. Nos gusta aprender, experimentar con nuevas ideas y afrontar desafíos que nos permitan salir de nuestra zona de confort.
Buscamos personas creativas, curiosas y con iniciativa, que disfruten trabajando en equipo y tengan ganas de aportar sus conocimientos, aprender de otros y convertir ideas en algo increíble.
summary:
Walkback is a mixed-reality prototype for Meta Quest 3 that answers one question for an astronaut walking on Mars: can I still walk back to the habitat?

It puts a real square kilometre of Gale crater on a table in your room, built from the HiRISE 1 m elevation model and the HiRISE 25 cm photo. It plans a walk from the habitat to four sites where Curiosity drilled and back, never stepping on a slope over 20°, and shows the time, the oxygen and a verdict: VIABLE or NOT VIABLE. A WHAT IF drops the oxygen tank to test a suit failure and paints red the ground you could no longer walk back from. A mission mode puts you on the same terrain at real scale, with the headset standing in for a helmet display that counts the way back.

We are exact about what is data and what is not. The terrain is real and was checked against Curiosity's own tilt sensor. Every time and oxygen figure is labelled ESTIMATE on screen: it comes from a stand-in model over the real relief, not yet from a validated one. Walkback is a decision aid for planning a walk, not a game and not an operational tool.
details:
WHAT IT DOES TODAY

- Real Mars on a table. A Mars globe (Viking colour mosaic) lands on Gale crater and a 1 km x 1 km square of it sits on a table in the user's room (mixed reality, passthrough). The relief is the HiRISE 1 m elevation model; the photo is the HiRISE 25 cm mosaic.

- Four map layers: PHOTO, HEIGHT, SLOPE (ground over 20° hatched as no-go) and RETURN (minutes to walk back to the habitat from every point, over the relief).

- Four stops, all real Curiosity drill sites at the rover's own positions: Altadena, Valle de la Luna, Nevado Sajama and Campo Marte. Each stop card gives its science, from the NASA Curiosity blog, and its tasks with minutes.

- Route and verdict. The app plans habitat -> the four stops in order -> habitat over the relief and shows a verdict card with three charts: oxygen tank, time, and height along the route. Today's plan (ESTIMATE): VIABLE, 1.8 km, 43 min walking, 2 h 12 min of work at the stops, 2 h 55 min in total, 181 L of oxygen = 36 % of the 497 L tank, 285 L spare above the 31 L reserve.

- WHAT IF. One click re-plans with the tank at 15 %, then at 8 %. At 15 % the verdict is NOT VIABLE but no ground is red yet. At 8 % the verdict is NOT VIABLE and 57.5 % of the ground that has a way back on foot turns red: from there the oxygen left no longer covers the walk back (ESTIMATE).

- Mission mode. START MISSION puts the user on the same terrain at 1:1 scale, with the route on the ground, a pillar and an arrival card at each stop, and jumps between stops. A helmet-style display shows the oxygen left, the minutes back to the habitat in green, amber or red, a compass, an arrow to the next stop, and TURN BACK NOW with a two-beep alert when the oxygen above the reserve no longer covers the way back. A room view keeps that display and the route over the real floor.

- Curiosity's 360° panorama at Nevado Sajama (Mastcam mosaic PIA26696) can be entered from that stop's card.

- Current conditions card: Curiosity's latest stored REMS weather report (sol 4995, Earth date 2026-08-25), season, daylight, surface radiation (Curiosity RAD) and the week's space weather, each with its source and date. One line can be live: at start, if the headset is online, the app asks NASA DONKI once for the solar particle events of the last 7 days and marks that line "(live)" with the UTC time of the check; with no usable answer it keeps the stored line, marked "(stored in the app)". Nothing on this card feeds the oxygen estimate.

HOW IT WORKS

- The stand-in model ("plan B"): each leg is the fastest way over the 257 x 257 elevation grid (Dijkstra, with Tobler's hiking function normalised to a flat-ground pace of 19.3 min/km, and no step on ground over 20°), then smoothed with straight shortcuts where they stay walkable. Walking spends oxygen per minute walked; work at a stop spends it at the suit's design rate. The verdict is VIABLE only if, at every stop, the oxygen above the reserve still covers the walk back.

- The scene is generated by code, and an automatic test builds it and checks it without the headset: 424 checks, all passing on 15 Nov 2026.

- The data package is built by scripts in the repository (data-pipeline/) that read only the 1 km window from the NASA and USGS servers. DATA.md lists every source, command and check.

WHAT WE CHECKED

- Terrain: the slopes of the elevation model differ from Curiosity's own tilt sensor by 2.0° on average at 85 rover positions (r = 0.77, largest difference 21°). That supports the terrain. It does not validate the oxygen numbers.

- In the headset (Meta Quest 3, 15 Nov 2026, read from the app's own log): 72 fps at the table and on Mars at 1:1 scale; the terrain and its layers, the verdict board, the 360° photo, mission mode, the room view and the live NASA DONKI line were seen working. The jumps between stops, the arrival card and TURN BACK NOW pass the automatic test; the README's status table says what had been tried in the headset.

WHY IT MATTERS

On a surface walk the question is not how far you can go; it is whether you can still come back. Walkback keeps that answer in sight while a walk is planned and while it is walked, on real relief, and says plainly which numbers are estimates. A team can compare science stops and see when one more stop puts the return at risk.

TOOLS

Unity 6000.4.6f1 (C#, Universal Render Pipeline 17.4.0), Meta XR SDK 209.0.0, OpenXR Plugin 1.16.1, Input System 1.19.0; hardware: Meta Quest 3. Data: Python, GDAL 3.13.3 and QGIS 3.44.15.

USE OF AI (declared in full in AI_USAGE.md in the repository)

- Code: Claude Code (Anthropic) wrote the app's C# scripts, the data-pipeline scripts, the automatic test and the build tools, under the team's direction. The first line of every script says so: "Written with Claude Code (AI), directed and tested by team MARSXR". It also ran review rounds and wrote patches; the team chose which ones to apply.

- Research: Gemini (Google) and Grok (xAI) were used in one research round on candidate stops and data sources. Every position was then checked against Curiosity's waypoints and every line against the NASA Curiosity blog.

- Documents: README, DATA.md, NOTICE, AI_USAGE.md and the drafts of this form were written with Claude Code and reviewed by the team.

- Images, video and audio: none is AI-generated in the app, in the repository or in the demo video. Every image is NASA or USGS data, or a rendering of that data by our own code; the app's sounds are generated by code. No AI-written content uses a NASA logo or insignia.

- The team chose the problem, the site, the stops and the data sources, decided on every proposal the AI made, ran the app on the Meta Quest 3 and reported what worked and what did not.

LIMITS

- Time and oxygen are an ESTIMATE: Tobler's function was measured on Earth without a suit; the model has no suit metabolic model, no sand and no gravity term. Its constants are the prototype's settings; the repository's NOTICE file lists them and says where each one comes from.

- The route grid is about 3.9 m: rocks and steps smaller than that are not on the map, and there is no sand map.

- The Mars weather report is stored and dated; it is not downloaded when the app runs.

- The habitat's position is the team's proposal (a point on Curiosity's own path); there is no habitat there.

- One site (Gale). Not an operational tool.

NEXT STEPS (NOT DONE)

- Replace the stand-in with a validated walking and oxygen model, and test with people whether the alerts are read correctly.

- Read a suit's telemetry instead of estimating it, which is the kind of problem the NASA SUITS challenge sets. Walkback reads no suit telemetry today.

Code and APK: https://github.com/kendal-dev/Walkback (Apache 2.0; the APK is on the Releases page, tag v1.0-submission). NASA does not endorse this project; no NASA logo or insignia is used.
